 14|# FigJam Type - User Flow
 15|
 16|A user flow is the screens and choices one person passes through to reach a goal. It is the default Flow type and the strictest, because it is drawn from screenshots and frames a reader will compare node by node.
 17|
 18|**Loading Condition:** CONDITIONAL, when the Flow route draws a user flow
 19|**Purpose:** The grammar, rules, budget and read-back for a user flow
 20|**Pairs With:** `assets/flow-templates.md`
 21|
 22|---
 23|
 24|## 1. WHEN TO USE
 25|
 26|**The reader's question:** which screens does a person pass through, and where do they choose?
 27|
 28|- A flow drawn from screenshots, from Figma frames or from a product doc that walks one person through the product
 29|- A platform split, such as desktop and mobile, that rejoins on a later screen
 30|- A journey, which Flow Mode does not draw as such, redrawn as the screens it visits
 31|
 32|Use another type when several people or teams hand work to each other (a process), when the subject is services and stores (an architecture) or when time order between systems is the point (a sequence).
 33|
 34|---
 35|
 36|## 2. WHAT THE BOARD DRAWS
 37|
 38|`flowchart LR` or `flowchart TD`, composed into a board as Section 6 sets out. No `%% type:` line is needed, because a flowchart with none is a user flow.
 39|
 40|| Shape | Mermaid | Means |
 41||---|---|---|
 42|| Stadium | `id([Label])` | The flow starts or ends here |
 43|| Rectangle | `id[Label]` | A screen or an action |
 44|| Rhombus | `id{Label?}` | A choice, written as a question |
 45|| Circle | `id((.))` | A merge dot, where branches rejoin, with no words |
 46|
 47|Every connector is a solid one-way arrow, `-->`, with an optional label: `a -->|Yes| b`.
 48|
 49|On the board the first screen takes the `entry` role, every other screen the `neutral` role, a decision a diamond in the `decision` role, the goal the `goal` role and every other end the `exit` role, beside the main line rather than on it, and `assets/figjam-design.md` names the swatch each role draws. The main route from the first screen to the goal runs on one straight line, and `%% zone:` lines group the screens into named stages, as `assets/flow-templates.md` Section 1 sets out.
 50|
 51|Every move carries an actor in the model, one of a person, a system or a timer. A system step is marked automatic and a timer step is fired by time, so neither is ever counted as a missing user action.
 52|
 53|---
 54|
 55|## 3. RULES
 56|
 57|The check enforces:
 58|
 59|- **Four shapes only.** No other shape, no subgraph and never a colour per type. A `%% zone:` line does the grouping instead
 60|- **A decision has 1 to 3 exits, each labelled.** A fourth outcome means the decision is two decisions
 61|- **Every node connected, every step with a way in and a way out.** Only a stadium starts or ends the flow, and a stadium never sits mid-flow. The first node may take a loop back to it
 62|- **A merge dot carries no words**
 63|- **Solid one-way arrows only.** A dotted, thick, headless or two-way connector would carry a second meaning. A proposal's status goes in its label, and a `style` line marks the goal
 64|- **Left to right or top to bottom,** the same way for every diagram of one flow. Left to right is the default, because the composer keeps the main route on one straight line across a board that reads wider than tall and sets each branch beside it. Top to bottom suits a short flow
 65|- **Labels of at most 40 characters on one line,** in double quotes when they hold a parenthesis, a colon or a slash
 66|- **camelCase ids,** never an underscore or a reserved word such as `end`
 67|- **No emoji, markup or literal `\n`** anywhere in the block but a `%%` comment
 68|- **At most 9 nodes,** and exactly one `style` line from `references/style-guide.md`
 69|
 70|Judged by hand:
 71|
 72|- **Labels name the screen or the action in the product's own words,** one to four words where those words allow
 73|- **A decision label is a question and each exit one of its answers**
 74|- **Exits read the same way across the flow,** such as Yes to the right and No below, so a reader learns the pattern once
 75|- **The shape carries the type, so the label does not repeat it.** Write `valid{Card valid?}`, never `valid{Decision: card valid?}`
 76|- **A state is a screen in another condition, and no fifth shape carries it.** A state earns its own node only when a different action reaches it or a reader can be trapped in it, and otherwise the condition goes in the screen's label and under `Left out:`
 77|
 78|---
 79|
 80|## 4. BUDGET AND SPLITTING
 81|
 82|Nine nodes is sk-design-diagram's general budget and matches what a hand-drawn user flow uses. A longer flow splits into diagrams that hand off through a named end and a start with the same label, all in one file. Every source step lands in one diagram or under `Left out:`, never dropped silently. At `Meeting screen` distance labels drop to 32 characters. At `Wall` distance the budget drops to 6 nodes, with labels at 25 characters, as the reading distance dial in `references/flow-mode.md` Section 4 sets out.
 83|
 84|---
 85|
 86|## 5. COLOUR, ZONES AND NOTES
 87|
 88|The composer colours every screen by its kind. A user flow and a process each carry exactly one `style` line, which marks the first glance. A styled goal, failing end or decision keeps its kind and takes the accent's outline. A styled step is drawn in the accent's pair. The line marks meaning: on an end it makes that end the goal, or with the light red pair a failure, and on a screen it puts that screen in focus, as `references/style-guide.md` Section 3 sets out. Zones are `%% zone:` lines in flow order, and once a flow has zones every screen sits in one. A note on a screen, such as a drop-off rate, goes on through the pins and legend recipe in `references/hybrid-workflow.md`.
 89|
 90|---
 91|
 92|## 6. WRITING THE BOARD
 93|
 94|`scripts/compose_board.py` composes the model and one `use_figma` call draws the board, as `references/flow-mode.md` Section 6 sets out. On the generated fallback, `generate_diagram` takes `name`, `mermaidSyntax` and `userIntent`, with `name` set to the flow and its hand-off and no `useArchitectureLayoutCode`. The `fj` route can also draw a user flow when neither hosted tool is connected.
 95|
 96|---
 97|
 98|## 7. READ-BACK
 99|
100|Count on the board, against the model: nodes, connectors, decision exits labelled, every node label, and for each model connector a board connector joining the same two nodes in the same direction with the same label, following a routed edge through its legs as `references/flow-mode.md` Section 7 sets out. When the flow has zones, each screen sits in its zone.
101|
102|```text
103|Read-back: 8 of 8 nodes, 8 of 8 connectors, 2 of 2 decision exits labelled
104|```
105|
106|---
107|
108|## 8. PATTERNS AND EXAMPLE
109|
110|- `assets/flow-templates.md` holds five user-flow patterns that pass the check
111|- `assets/examples/user-flow-fernhouse-return.md` walks one flow from screenshots to the reply

 92|- No meta-commentary about the writing process
 93|- No disclaimers or notes about tone choices
 94|- No reference to these rules
 95|- No explanation of why a word was avoided or replaced
 96|- No lines such as "I've kept this concise" or "I avoided jargon"
 97|- No knowledge-cutoff disclaimers or date hedging ("as of my last update", "based on available information", "while specific details are limited")
 98|- No training-data hedging ("Up to my last training update", "I don't have access to real-time data")
 99|
100|---
101|
102|## 9. STRUCTURAL BANS, WHAT NO SCANNER SEES
103|
104|- **"Not just X, but Y."** Every variant, "not only X but Y" included. State X. State Y separately
105|- **Triad density, never the triad itself.** A single three-item list is fine and needs no defence. What this flags is two or more of them inside 150 words, which reads as a tic. Fix that by merging or splitting a list whose content genuinely allows it, and prefer counts of 2, 4 or 5 where the count is yours to choose. Never invent a filler item, and never drop a real one, to move a count off three. A triad the source, the template or the subject fixes (a three-slot taxonomy, a three-value enum, three named states) is content, and padding it is a worse failure than the tic this rule exists to catch
106|- **Copula avoidance.** "serves as", "stands as", "functions as", "acts as", "boasts", "features", "offers". Write "is" or "has"
107|- **Synonym cycling.** Reaching for a second word for a thing you already named, so the prose looks varied. Pick one term and repeat it every time. Repeating a fixed label, an identifier or a template's own wording is this rule being obeyed, never a violation of it
108|- **False ranges.** "From X to Y" where the endpoints share no scale
109|- **Inline-header vertical lists.** A stack of bolded-header bullets in the bold-plus-colon shape. Rewrite as prose or a plain list. Allowed in glossaries, API docs and config guides
110|- **Generic conclusions.** "the future looks bright", "exciting times lie ahead", "a major step forward", "the possibilities are endless", "we look forward to what's next", "this is just the beginning", "the best is yet to come", "continue their journey toward excellence". End on a specific, or end
111|- **Fragmented headers.** A first sentence restating its heading. Cut it, open on substance
112|- **Significance inflation.** "marks a pivotal moment in", "setting the stage for", "indelible mark", "is a testament to", "underscores the importance of", "reflects broader trends in", "represents a shift in", "key turning point", "shaping the future of", "deeply rooted in", "symbolising its ongoing", "contributing to the". State what happened, then the evidence
113|- **Notability by association.** Listing three or more outlets without a specific claim, "active social media presence with over X followers", "has been featured in", "covered by major publications". Cite the specific coverage and what it said
114|- **Formulaic challenges sections.** "Despite its [quality], [subject] faces challenges typical of", "Despite these challenges, [subject] continues to thrive", "Challenges and Legacy", "Future Outlook", "faces several challenges, including". Give the specific facts
115|
116|---
117|
118|## 10. ALWAYS CUT
119|
120|Structural removals, not scored penalties. Cut the word, keep the sentence. These are edits, so they never count toward the hard blocker total.
121|
122|very, really, truly, absolutely, incredibly, extremely, quite, rather, somewhat, fairly, just, actually, basically, literally, simply, obviously, clearly, certainly, definitely, undoubtedly, essentially
123|
124|Never cut a semantic connective (because, so, unless, which means) to save words.
125|
126|---
127|
128|## 11. BEFORE DELIVERY
129|
130|Draft, reread as a skeptical human reader, fix, then report on the required line:
131|
132|`HVR self-scan: N hard blockers. Fixed: <terms>. Kept with reason: <terms>.`
133|
134|`N` counts hard blockers only: punctuation, blocker words, blocker phrases, metaphors, setup phrases, unfixed generalisations, output-warning leaks and structural bans. Always-cut modifiers are fixed in place and never counted.
135|
136|The line is delivery metadata. It belongs in the response beside the export path, never inside the artifact body, exactly as a Mode, Template, Perspectives, Quality Score or Energy header stays out of a delivered artifact. The output warnings above govern the artifact, so a scan reported inside it would break them. Reported in the response, it does not.

 13|
 14|# Rules - Conciseness
 15|
 16|The conciseness layer above the Human Voice card: what to cut, what is never cut, and the test that decides which is which.
 17|
 18|**Loading Condition:** ALWAYS, and rules only. A file paid for on every turn stays small enough to be worth paying for
 19|**Purpose:** Carries the cut rules, the keep rules and the reconstruction test that decides between them, so every delivery is sized as well as checked for banned wording
 20|**Scope:** Quantity, structure and load-bearing-ness, so an artifact that clears every hard blocker is not still three times too long. Nothing routes to it, since being ALWAYS-loaded is what makes it unroutable
 21|**Output Path:** None. The layer governs the length of an artifact another file writes, and produces none of its own
 22|**Loads With:** the consuming system's skill entry and `Rules - Human Voice Core`. That card governs word choice and this file governs quantity, so both run on every delivery
 23|**Authority:** `Rules - Conciseness - On Demand Rationale` carries the reason behind every rule below, the vocabulary candidates that were refused, the worked cut and keep pairs, and the roster of what blocks against what advises. Load it ON_DEMAND before changing a rule, never in order to write one. Both files share one numbering, so a section present in one and absent here lives there and keeps its number. That is why this card runs 5, 7, 8, 12 rather than counting straight, and why renumbering it would break the Section 8 citations three skills carry
 24|
 25|---
 26|
 27|## 1. THE TWO-SIDED CONTRACT
 28|
 29|Cuts and keeps here are edits rather than scored penalties, so they never count toward a system's hard blocker total. The two halves are load-bearing in equal measure: read only the cut half and the output arrives compressed until the reasoning falls out of it, and read only the keep half and nothing ever gets shorter. Every rule the validator blocks on arrives in a pair at the same strength, so the gate cannot be satisfied by cutting alone.
 30|
 31|---
 32|
 33|## 2. THE RECONSTRUCTION TEST
 34|
 35|After a cut, could a reader who does not already know the answer recover what was removed from what remains? If yes, the cut was free. If no, the information moved into the reader's head, which is loss wearing the shape of compression. Apply it per cut and never per document, because a document-level verdict is a judgement about length and length is the judgement that strips connectives. The reader it asks about is the one who opens the artifact three weeks later with no memory of the conversation that produced it.
 36|
 37|---
 38|
 39|## 3. CUT RULES
 40|
 41|### 3.1 The named rules
 42|
 43|- **Question echo.** An opening that restates the prompt before answering it
 44|- **Intent narration.** Announcing the move instead of making it
 45|- **Compliance acknowledgement.** Agreeing to do the work at the top of the work
 46|- **Terminal recap.** A closing paragraph that repeats the body, even accurately
 47|- **Hedge stack.** Two or more uncertainty markers on one claim. Keep the one that is true
 48|- **Importance assertion.** A sentence whose only content is that something matters
 49|- **The conclusion move.** The whole paragraph, not only the phrase that opens it
 50|- **Both-sides padding.** Symmetric pro and con on a question that is not symmetric
 51|- **Empty enumeration.** Naming that there are several things, listing them, analysing none
 52|- **Heading echo.** A first sentence that restates its own heading
 53|- **Restated constraint.** Repeating back a fact the user supplied
 54|- **Effort reporting.** Narrating the work done rather than what it found
 55|- **Count padding.** An item added so a list carries a different number of items. The triad rule counts triads per 150 words and bans none, so leave the count alone and cut something that was never load-bearing
 56|
 57|### 3.2 The stated vocabulary
 58|
 59|The validator blocks on exactly the terms below, so this list and the gate are one list, and adding a term to either alone is the drift that kept these checks advisory. Section 3.3 of the on-demand rationale records every candidate refused, with the correct writing each would have failed.
 60|
 61|Never open a sentence with: "In conclusion", "In summary", "To summarize", "To summarise", "To recap", "To sum up", "It's worth noting", "It is worth noting", "It's important to note", "It is important to note", "Let's explore", "Let's dive in", "Let's take a look", "At the end of the day", "Without further ado", "As we all know", "It goes without saying", "First and foremost", "Last but not least", "With that in mind", "On that note", "That said", "Needless to say", "Simply put", "In essence", "At its core", "In the world of", "When it comes to", "At a high level", "As you can see", "As mentioned above", "As noted above", "As previously noted", "As we have seen", "As discussed above", "In this section", "Put simply", "Generally speaking", "Broadly speaking", "The key takeaway", "The fact of the matter is", "It should be noted", "It must be noted", "By way of background".
 62|
 63|Never close a section on: "In summary", "In conclusion", "To summarize", "To summarise", "To recap", "To sum up", "In short", "All in all", "Overall", "Ultimately", "In closing", "To conclude", "To wrap up", "The takeaway", "Net net", "In a nutshell", "Long story short", "To put it simply", "On the whole".
 64|
 65|At most one hedge per claim: "might", "may", "could", "perhaps", "maybe", "possibly", "potentially", "probably", "seems", "appears", "arguably", "somewhat", "relatively", "presumably", "likely", "generally", "typically", "I think", "I believe", "tends to", "to some extent", "in some cases", "apparently", "conceivably", "ostensibly", "seemingly", "in theory", "I suspect", "My sense is".
 66|
 67|A cross-reference that names its target stays legitimate, so "As noted above" is banned while "the payout window defined under The weekly cycle" is not. A heading followed by a sentence that shares its words and adds no new one is a heading echo: cut the sentence and open on substance.
 68|
 69|### 3.4 The two cut rules the validator settles alone
 70|
 71|Both resolve without judgement, so the validator blocks on them in a deliverable and reports them as advice on an instruction file.
 72|
 73|**Importance assertion.** A sentence of twelve words or fewer carrying one of "important", "critical", "essential", "crucial", "vital", "matters", "significant", "noteworthy" or "fundamental", and carrying no content word of its own beyond that marker and generic filler. A sentence that names what matters and why is left alone.
 74|
 75|**Effort reporting.** A sentence opening on "I" or "We" that reaches one of "analysed", "analyzed", "reviewed", "checked", "scored", "scanned", "verified", "examined", "evaluated", "assessed", "investigated" or "audited" within the next few words. A quoted mention is left alone, and so is a sentence whose subject is the process the artifact documents rather than the author. State what the work found, since the work itself is not the deliverable.
 76|
 77|---
 78|
 79|## 4. KEEP RULES
 80|
 81|The anti-robotic half, at the same weight as the cut list. Each item names what a compression pass destroys first.
 82|
 83|- **Semantic connectives.** `because`, `so`, `which means`, `unless`, `otherwise`, `since` carry the logic, and deleting one turns an argument into a pile of assertions. The Human Voice cap on `however`, `furthermore`, `moreover`, `additionally` and `consequently` limits rhetoric and never reaches these
 84|- **One concrete instance per non-obvious rule.** The example is what makes a rule applicable
 85|- **The caveat that prevents a wrong action.** A reader who follows the trimmed version and breaks something was not served by the trim
 86|- **The scope qualifier.** `when`, `only when`, `for X but not Y`. A rule stripped of its scope is applied everywhere
 87|- **The noun behind a pronoun.** Name it again once the referent sits more than a clause away
 88|- **The negative case.** "A path string is not verification" is where the reader learns the boundary
 89|- **The specific number.** 33 fixtures, not several fixtures
 90|- **One human beat per roughly 400 words.** An aside, a judgement, a plain admission of what is unknown
 91|- **Grammar.** Articles, copulas and finite verbs are never a compression target, because conciseness removes claims and never syntax
 92|
 93|---
 94|
 95|## 5. OVER-COMPRESSION SIGNATURES
 96|
 97|### 5.1 The five shapes
 98|
 99|- **Connective stripping.** Clauses sit next to each other with the relation deleted, so the reader guesses whether the second causes, qualifies or contradicts the first
100|- **Referent stripping.** Pronouns and bare nouns left with their antecedents cut away
101|- **Telegraphese.** Dropped articles and copulas, verbless fragments, headline grammar in body text
102|- **Condition collapse.** A conditional rule flattened into an absolute one, which is a correctness bug rather than a style one
103|- **Example deletion.** An abstract rule left with nothing showing what it looks like in use
104|
105|### 5.2 The two the validator counts, and the perimeter they are measured over
106|
107|Connective stripping and telegraphese leave a numeric trace, so the validator counts them and blocks on a deliverable below either floor. Repair a document that trips one by naming the deleted relations back in and restoring the subject behind every stranded pronoun, never by adding words.
108|
109|- **Connective floor.** At least 5 semantic connectives per 1000 words of prose
110|- **Article floor.** At least 30 articles per 1000 words of prose
111|
112|Both floors are measured over paragraph prose alone, because a ratio only means something where sentences carry the reasoning. Outside the perimeter: frontmatter, a heading at any level, a bullet, a numbered item, a table row, a blockquote, an image, a horizontal rule, a field line such as `**Placement:** Creator deals dashboard`, a hashtag or handle run, a label line whose whole content is one bold or underlined run such as `**Most authentic**`, anything inside a fenced code block, and any HTML comment. Below 200 words of paragraph prose neither floor is applied, since a ratio over fewer words than that is noise.
113|
114|---
115|
116|## 7. FORMAT
117|
118|Prose, bullets and tables are not interchangeable, and picking wrong is how a short answer still reads badly. Three questions decide and the first yes wins: prose where the items differ in weight or their order encodes reasoning, a table where every row shares the same fields, bullets where the items are parallel, independently actionable and three to seven in number. Anything reaching the end without a yes is one paragraph pretending to be a list. Over-bulleting is the main way output turns robotic while looking concise, and the tells are verbless fragments, a bullet that needs the one above it to parse, and a list whose connectives were deleted so the items would line up. Heading density scales with length: under 300 words no headings, above that one per 150 to 400 words.
119|
120|---
121|
122|## 8. WHAT A DELIVERABLE NEVER CONTAINS
123|
124|The reasoning that produced an artifact, the score it earned and the assumptions it rests on are real work, and they belong in the reply beside the export path rather than inside the file the reader opens.
125|
126|### 8.1 The enumeration
127|
128|- A scoring section of any kind, whether headed MEQT, HVR, DEAL scoring, Scoring, Self-scan, Hard blockers or Weakest
129|- A dimension breakdown line, such as `M 4 · E 6 · Q 6 · T 3 · D 3` or its `D · E · A · L` equivalent
130|- A total, a floor status, a pass or fail verdict, or a score band action
131|- A hard blocker count or a voice self-scan line, in any wording
132|- Score commentary, such as a line opening `Weakest:` and naming which dimensions were thin
133|- An improvement-cycle note, an iteration count or a re-score history
134|- A bracketed `[Assumes: ...]` tag
135|- A methodology transcript, a perspective roster, an energy level or a phase-flow trace
136|- A validation checklist, a gate roster or a template-compliance report
137|- An attestation footer, a Mode header in visible text, a Template version in visible text, or any other processing metadata
138|
139|### 8.2 The one sanctioned exception
140|
141|Line 1 may carry a single HTML comment header, which renders as nothing and is the designed home for the mode, the framework, the score and the template version. A `Stats:` or `Assumes:` line written as an HTML comment directly below sits inside the same exception, for the same reason. Invisible when rendered is the whole test, so a score written as visible text is a violation wherever it sits in the file and a score written as a comment is fine wherever it sits.
142|
143|### 8.3 Where the reporting goes instead
144|
145|The reply carries what the artifact does not: the export path with read-back confirmation where the runtime can write files, the score and its verdict at the depth the mode calls for, the voice self-scan line naming the terms fixed and the terms kept with their reason, the assumptions in a form the user can correct before they harden, a short summary and one next step. Producing that report is the point, and moving it out of the artifact does not make it optional.
146|
147|### 8.4 Two narrow overrides
148|
149|Where the artifact refines a supplied source, never inject a Mode, Template, Perspectives, Quality Score or Energy header into preserved source structure, since the comment header is for a new artifact and a refinement keeps the source's own opening. Where the packaging renders the deliverable in a panel instead of saving a file, that rendered block is the artifact and the enumeration applies to it unchanged, the report follows the block, and the path is reported as export-equivalent rather than claimed as a save.
150|
151|---
152|
153|## 12. THE PRE-EXPORT PASS
154|
155|Run this after the voice pass and before the export, in order. The first two steps are the cut side and the last three are the keep side, and running only the cut side is the failure this layer exists to prevent.
156|
157|1. Delete every opener, recap and hedge stack named in Section 3.2, both shapes named in Section 3.4, and the question echo, intent narration, compliance acknowledgement and closing recap the body already carries, including the sentences after the phrase that opened one
158|2. Apply the reconstruction test to every remaining cut you are tempted to make, and stop at the first one that fails
159|3. Name every relation a reader would otherwise guess, then repair referent stripping, telegraphese and condition collapse in place
160|4. Confirm one concrete instance survives per non-obvious rule, one caveat survives per action that could go wrong, and the format matches the content under Section 7
161|5. Confirm the body carries nothing from Section 8.1, and that everything removed at this step now sits in the reply. This step is skipped most often, because the process material was correct work and deleting correct work feels wrong. It is not deleted, it moves
</file-view>

 15|# FigJam Diagram Quality Rubric
 16|
 17|The script checks what a script can see. This rubric is the rest: whether the diagram should exist, whether every node earns its place and whether the reader can trust what lands on the board. Walk it after the check passes and before the write gate.
 18|
 19|**Loading Condition:** CONDITIONAL, on every Flow route before the write gate
 20|**Purpose:** The judgement pass between the pre-write check and the gate
 21|**Scope:** The model, the provenance table, the planned extensions and, after the write, the board and the reply
 22|
 23|---
 24|
 25|## 1. TYPE FIT
 26|
 27|- [ ] The type answers the reader's question, as `references/flow-mode.md` Section 3 maps it
 28|- [ ] A table, a list or a paragraph would not do the same job. If it would, say so and offer that instead
 29|- [ ] The type's reference in `references/types/` was loaded and its judged-by-hand rules were applied
 30|- [ ] A request for a kind Flow Mode does not draw was answered with the nearest type it does draw, or a plain no
 31|
 32|---
 33|
 34|## 2. THE REMOVE TEST
 35|
 36|sk-design-diagram's highest-quality move is usually deletion. A diagram is done when nothing can be removed.
 37|
 38|The remove test runs on the outline before the first Mermaid block, because a step cut from a list of steps costs a sentence and the same step cut from a drawn diagram costs a redraw. This section is the third rung of the challenge ladder in `references/flow-mode.md` Section 3, so the two rungs above it are asked first: what the board must not do, and whether a list, a table or a paragraph would serve the reader better.
 39|
 40|- [ ] The `userIntent` sentence was agreed in the sparring and is the first line of the outline, rather than composed at the write call
 41|- [ ] The remove test ran on the outline, one line per node and edge, before any layout was judged
 42|- [ ] An unanswered sparring proposal is marked assumed and named in the playback before the gate
 43|- [ ] No node can be removed without the reader losing a step they need
 44|- [ ] Every node serves the `userIntent` sentence, or it is cut and named under `Left out:`
 45|- [ ] No two nodes always travel together. If they do, they are one node
 46|- [ ] No connector restates what the layout already shows
 47|- [ ] No label repeats what the shape already says
 48|- [ ] No diagram carries the same label on four or more connectors. Cut them all, or keep one where the label says something the shape cannot. Decision exits and sequence messages are exempt, and an architecture renames each edge instead, as its type reference sets out
 49|- [ ] The remove test ran on the outline before the first Mermaid block, so no node was drawn only to be cut
 50|- [ ] The diagram sits inside its budget, or was split, and every cut is named under `Left out:`
 51|
 52|---
 53|
 54|## 3. SIGNAL
 55|
 56|The marked node is chosen against a target written down first. A board judged only against itself cannot catch a second focal object, such as a title that repeats the claim the marked node was meant to carry. Three lines are written before the first Mermaid block:
 57|
 58|1. **First glance.** The one claim, decision or object that should win within two seconds
 59|2. **Second glance.** The evidence or relationship that advances it
 60|3. **Last glance.** The risk, the metadata or the appendix that stays available without competing
 61|
 62|Those three lines travel into the gate, so the marked node is chosen from them and the reply can say what should win. After the first glance, filled shapes and their keyed fills outweigh connector labels and text in the overview, so the lines name a filled group such as the gray end states before the labels between them.
 63|
 64|- [ ] One accent on a user flow or a process, on the node a reader would keep if they could keep only one, never the node that comes first. The goal, a failure end, a decision and the one step in focus are the candidates, as `references/style-guide.md` Section 3 sets out. Two that tie mean the diagram splits
 65|- [ ] The three glance lines were written before the model and named in the gate
 66|- [ ] On a user flow or a process the first glance is the accented node, marked by the one `style` line the check requires, and the gate names it. On any other type it is the node, message or task a `%% focus:` line names, or, when the model has none, whatever the layout shows first, and the gate says which. The first glance is one node, message or task, never a group such as the end states, and when the layout would show another first, a `%% focus:` line marks it, so the gate never promises a first glance the board does not show. It is the claim the reader came for rather than the node the flow reaches first, and nothing the second or last glance owns competes with it
 67|- [ ] No title repeats the focal claim, so one idea carries one focal object. Where the title already states the claim, the marked node carries the evidence, the consequence or the next move
 68|- [ ] The title names what the reader is looking at, the subtitle says in one sentence who reads it and why, and the source line names the sources and what was left out
 69|- [ ] Shape and label carry the meaning on their own, so the diagram reads in greyscale
 70|- [ ] The key the composer draws names every kind, line and arrow the board shows and nothing else, and no note adds a second key beside it
 71|- [ ] Every zone carries a name a reader can see, and zones group what belongs together rather than marking a position
 72|- [ ] Every label uses the product's or the source's own words. Proper nouns are never renamed
 73|- [ ] The naming fits the audience: exact component names for engineers, plain verbs for a mixed team, capabilities and outcomes for leadership
 74|- [ ] Nothing was invented to fill a lane, a slot or a gap. A missing step is asked about or named, never guessed
 75|
 76|---
 77|
 78|## 4. PROVENANCE
 79|
 80|- [ ] Every node has a row in the provenance table naming its source and its source class
 81|- [ ] Nothing marked proposal or unknown is drawn as current behavior. Its status sits in its label, or it is left out
 82|- [ ] Every causal edge is stated by its sources from both ends. An edge one source states and another contradicts is a finding, not a connector
 83|- [ ] A contradicted item leaves a trace the reader can see. It sits in the reply's `Left out:` line with both sources and the reason, or the one question that asks which source governs settled it. Nothing is removed in silence and no extra line is invented for it
 84|
 85|---
 86|
 87|## 5. THE CHECK AND THE GATE
 88|
 89|- [ ] `scripts/flow_check.py` printed `PASSED` for the model file, with the type each diagram was read as
 90|- [ ] The measures printed beside the counts were read: the widest rank, the longest path, the connectors per step, the average label length and the crossing pairs, against the budgets `scripts/figjam_checks/layout.py` sets
 91|- [ ] A measure out of band was fixed in the model rather than on the board and the check rerun after the change, because the composer owns the layout and a tangled shape is never rearranged after the write
 92|- [ ] `scripts/compose_board.py` printed `COMPOSED` for every diagram, with the counts the read-back will look for
 93|- [ ] The gate message names the plan, the file, what will be written, any planned extensions, the calls the write will spend and the rollback
 94|- [ ] On the generated fallback, an architecture call carries `useArchitectureLayoutCode`, and no other type carries it
 95|
 96|---
 97|
 98|## 6. THE BOARD
 99|
100|After the write, before the reply:
101|
102|- [ ] The read-back counts match the model, as the type's reference sets them out
103|- [ ] Each provenance row whose class is not current behavior or whose edge is inferred was re-read against its source before the gate, and the row records the reason. A row that quotes a source line was not re-read
104|- [ ] The write returned no warning, and its counts match the counts the model expects
105|- [ ] The `COMPOSED` line named the design the board was drawn in, and each `DESIGN` warning it counted became a `Finding:` line naming the token and the shipped value the board used instead
106|- [ ] The overview is the screenshot the composing call returned, and `get_figjam` supplies the outline with a screenshot of each node
107|- [ ] A node that needs its own view is read with `get_screenshot` and a node id from that read, because the tool fails without one
108|- [ ] Two screenshots of the board were taken for this pass: one of the whole board in a single frame and one at 100% zoom. Composition is judged on the overview, because a crossing and a crowded label are invisible at reading size
109|- [ ] The overview reads in the order the model plans, and that order was written down before the first screenshot
110|- [ ] The overview shows no connector crossing another, no connector or label on a zone title, no two edges sharing a trunk the model draws apart and no two labels touching
111|- [ ] No edge runs through a zone it neither starts nor ends in. Edges that only arrive may share one magnet and then lie together for no more than 200 pixels
112|- [ ] One screenshot of the diagram shows no stretched shape, no label cut off and no overlap with existing board content
113|- [ ] Every gap a note or a person placed falls in one of the three bands `references/style-guide.md` Section 7 states, and two unrelated groups sit no closer than the text blocks inside a card
114|- [ ] Each zone holds its own nodes and no other, and no zone overlaps another
115|- [ ] The same screenshot shows no connector crossing and no edge that reads as joining the wrong node. Each edge is followed by eye from end to end, because a connector count does not prove that a route is clear
116|- [ ] Every colour on the board matches its entry in the key, the marked node sits where Section 3 places it, and the board answers the `userIntent` sentence without the model beside it
117|- [ ] Every fill on the board resolves to a role in the active design, as `assets/figjam-design.md` holds it, no zone tint shares a hue with a kind inside it or with the accent, and no note added a colour the design does not name
118|- [ ] The marked node reads first, and no other node competes with it
119|- [ ] A screenshot finding is reported, and it is fixed only by reshaping the model and composing again after a yes, inside the two-attempt bound `references/flow-mode.md` Section 9 sets
120|- [ ] Each extension landed where planned and covers no composed node's label
121|- [ ] Nothing was moved, resized or restyled after the write
122|- [ ] Every finding below full marks names the label it sits on, where it sits in the frame, and one fix, which is a model change composed again after a yes or a named composer limit the writer cannot move
123|
124|---
125|
126|## 7. THE DESIGN RUBRIC
127|
128|The checklists above decide whether a board may ship. The design rubric scores how well it reads, so two boards of the same model, or a board before and after a change, can be compared on something firmer than a glance. Score the overview screenshot on nine criteria, each 0, 1 or 2, for a total out of 18. A criterion scores 2 when it holds everywhere on the board, 1 when it holds with one named exception and 0 when it fails in two places or more.
129|
130|| Criterion | Scores 2 when |
131||---|---|
132|| Frame and entry | The board is one framed area with a title, a one-sentence subtitle and one obvious place to start reading |
133|| Reading order | The flow runs in one direction, the main route sits on one straight line and every branch sits beside it rather than across it |
134|| Colour by meaning | Every colour names a kind the key explains, and nothing is coloured for looks or by position |
135|| Grouping | Zones, lanes or composite states group what belongs together, each carries a visible name and neighbouring tints differ |
136|| Legibility | At overview zoom every label reads, no text is cut off or crowded and shapes of one kind share one size |
137|| Connector clarity | No connector crosses another or runs through a node or a zone title, two edges never lie on one stretch long enough to carry a label, every label sits on its own edge and clear of every other line and every end joins its node cleanly |
138|| Key and source | The key names every mark and nothing else, and the source line names the sources and what was left out |
139|| Proportion | The board reads wider than tall or close to square, with no tall strip, no large empty region and margins on the grid |
140|| Matches the active design | Every kind draws the pair its role names in `assets/figjam-design.md`, the title block and type sizes match every other board, the key lists its entries in the design's order with the focus last, every line takes the design's look and no zone tint shares a hue with a kind inside it |
141|
142|Every score below 2 names the label or the zone it sits on and one fix, in the same shape Section 6 asks of a finding. A comparison between two boards scores both on the same nine criteria and reports both totals, criterion by criterion, so a gain on one criterion never hides a loss on another.
143|
144|---
145|
146|## 8. THE REPLY
147|
148|- [ ] The board URL first, then the `Read-back:` line, then any `Extensions:` and `Left out:` lines, then any `Finding:` lines, then the `HVR self-scan:` line, with no text after it
149|- [ ] No sentence or key entry ties a colour or a zone tint to a team
150|- [ ] A mismatch is reported as measured, and the board is never called done on one
151|- [ ] No file was written to `export/`, and no Mermaid, HTML, SVG or PNG file was left behind

 19|This is the product-owner hub's second-layer router, at the hub root beside [`SKILL.md`](SKILL.md).  16|# FigJam Diagram Style Guide
 17|
 18|The rules for colour, type and spacing on a FigJam board. The composer in `assets/compose-board.js` draws every board in the design `assets/figjam-design.md` holds, which ships as the tables below record, and every hex a model, a design or a note extension uses comes from the palette in Section 3. `scripts/flow_check.py` refuses any other.
 19|
 20|**Loading Condition:** CONDITIONAL, before the gate on every Flow route, and when a model or a note extension uses colour
 21|**Purpose:** Names the colour each kind draws in, the type scale, the grid, the palette pairs the check accepts and the measured contrast record
 22|**Scope:** The composed board, Mermaid `style`, `classDef` and `linkStyle` colours, sticky and pin colours for notes, and the contrast record the self-test re-measures
 23|
 24|---
 25|
 26|## 1. OVERVIEW
 27|
 28|sk-design-diagram owns a skinnable palette with semantic roles and a record of where each value comes from. A FigJam board already has a palette of its own, and a colour the board recognises as a palette swatch can be recoloured from FigJam's colour picker by anyone on the board. So this guide does not skin the board. It picks FigJam's own pairs, gives each kind of node one of them and records what each pair measures.
 29|
 30|Three rules carry the board:
 31|
 32|- **Colour by meaning.** A kind fixes a node's shape and colour together, so a goal is light green and a decision light yellow on every board, whichever type draws them. A colour never marks a position in the layout and is never picked for looks
 33|- **The key names every colour.** The composer draws one key under the diagram, with a sample of every kind, line and arrow the board uses and nothing else, so a reader never meets a colour the board does not explain
 34|- **Colour never carries meaning alone.** Most kinds also differ by shape, such as a diamond for a decision or a cylinder for a data store. Where two kinds share a shape and differ only by colour, such as a goal and an exit, the label names the outcome and the key names both, so a reader who cannot tell the fills apart still reads the board
 35|
 36|The board's look is a design a team can change. `assets/figjam-design.md` holds it as tokens: the palette pair each colour role draws, the role each kind takes, the accent, the type sizes, the line colours, the zone tints and the words on the key. The tables below record the shipped design. A design that changes a token changes the board and not this guide, and a token that breaks a gate in Section 4 or a floor in that file's Section 7 falls back to its shipped value with a warning.
 37|
 38|The board carries one accent, by default a heavy pink outline on the node, message or task the first glance names. A user flow or a process marks it with a `style` line and the check refuses a model that has none. The other five types may name it with a `%% focus:` line. A `style` line does not colour a node for the board. It tells the composer what the node means, as Section 3 sets out.
 39|
 40|---
 41|
 42|## 2. KINDS
 43|
 44|The composer reads each node's kind from the model: its shape, its place in the flow, its lane, its stereotype or its `style` line. The kind fixes the shape and the pair, and the key names it in the words below.
 45|
 46|### Flows and processes
 47|
 48|| Kind | Shape | Colour | Key | Read from |
 49||---|---|---|---|---|
 50|| Start | Rounded rectangle | Light blue | Where it starts | A stadium node no edge enters |
 51|| Screen or step | Rounded rectangle | White | Screen or step, or Step on a process | A plain node |
 52|| Decision | Diamond | Light yellow | Decision | A rhombus |
 53|| Goal | Rounded rectangle | Light green | Goal reached | A styled end, or the end the longest path reaches when none is styled |
 54|| Exit | Rounded rectangle | Light orange | Leaves the flow | Every other unstyled end |
 55|| Error | Rounded rectangle | Light red | Error or blocked | An end styled with the light red pair |
 56|| Focus | Rounded rectangle | Light pink, 8 pixel outline | In focus | A styled step that is none of the kinds above |
 57|| Merge | 24 pixel dot | Dark gray | Paths join | A circle |
 58|| Data store | Cylinder | Light violet | Data store | A cylinder |
 59|| Sub-process | Predefined process | White | Sub-process | A subroutine |
 60|| Input or output | Parallelogram | Light teal | Input or output | A parallelogram |
 61|
 62|An exit and an error sit beside the main line rather than on it, so the longest route to the goal stays one straight line.
 63|
 64|The accent is not a kind. A styled goal, error, decision or any other node keeps the kind and fill it has and takes the pink outline on top, so a goal stays green and reads first. Only a styled step has no kind of its own to keep, so it is drawn light pink. The key adds `In focus` whenever the board carries an accent, and its sample is drawn as the marked node is, its own kind under the pink outline, so a goal in focus shows a green sample and a styled step a light pink one.
 65|
 66|### Architecture
 67|
 68|The lane a part sits in fixes its kind: a client is light teal, an edge or gateway light blue, a service white, a queue or stream an orange queue shape, a data store a violet cylinder and an outside system light gray.
 69|
 70|### State, ER, sequence and gantt
 71|
 72|| Kind | Shape | Colour | Key |
 73||---|---|---|---|
 74|| Initial and final pseudo-state | 32 pixel dot, the final one ringed | Charcoal | Start, End |
 75|| First state, a state, final state | Rounded rectangle | Light blue, white, light gray | First state, State, Final state |
 76|| Choice | 56 pixel diamond | Light yellow | Choice |
 77|| Fork or join | 16 by 96 pixel bar | Charcoal | Fork or join |
 78|| Entity | Card with its fields | White | Entity |
 79|| Participant | Rounded rectangle, drawn again smaller at the foot of its lifeline | White | Participant |
 80|| Planned, in progress, done, critical | Bar, the planned one outlined in the connector gray and the critical one with a heavier outline and `, critical` after its length | White, light blue, light gray, light red | Planned, In progress, Done, Critical, heavy outline |
 81|| Milestone | 32 pixel diamond | Light yellow | Milestone |
 82|
 83|A sequence numbers every message with a pin in the `marker` role, violet as shipped, beside its sender's lifeline, and its key names the pin `Step number`.
 84|
 85|### Lines and zones
 86|
 87|| Element | Colour | Notes |
 88||---|---|---|
 89|| Connector | Gray `#757575`, 2 pixels | Dashed for an optional or proposed edge, and for an async or outside call on an architecture |
 90|| Request, reply | Gray solid and gray dashed, both with a closed head | Sequence |
 91|| Async message, async reply | Blue `#3DADFF`, solid or dashed, with an open head | Sequence |
 92|| Lifeline | Light gray `#B3B3B3`, dashed | Sequence |
 93|| Accent | Pink `#F849C1`, 8 pixels around a node or bar and 4 pixels along a sequence message | The only pink and the only heavy line on a board |
 94|| Relationship | Gray, solid when identifying and dashed when not, no arrow | ER, with the cardinality in the label |
 95|| Zone | A section in a light tint, named in 24 pixel type | Tints cycle blue, orange, teal, yellow and violet. A zone skips a tint any kind inside it draws and the tint of any zone beside it, so a tint never hides its members and two neighbouring zones never read as one. A gantt section takes its band the same way |
 96|| Key | A light gray section under the diagram and as wide as it | One sample per mark the board uses, in one order on every board of a type with the focus last, wrapping onto a new row at the diagram's edge |
 97|| Board | A white section around everything | Named after the title |
 98|

100|
101|## 3. PALETTE
102|
103|### Accent and lane pairs
104|
105|The check accepts exactly the pairs in this record. Each fill takes only the stroke FigJam pairs it with, and a connector takes either the stroke or nothing. The lane pair is Figma's own suggestion for a diagram's one container, and it never counts as the accent. The composer draws every kind from the same pairs, with white for the plain kinds, charcoal for the pseudo-states, dark gray for the merge dot and the violet label preset for the pins. The light pink pair is the accent's and no kind draws it. A design may give the accent another pair, and then that pair is the accent's alone.
106|
107|The two ratio columns are measured: dark text on the fill against the 4.5:1 text gate, and the stroke on a white canvas against the 3.0:1 mark gate. `scripts/flow_check.py --self-test` re-measures every row and fails when a number or a pair drifts.
108|
109|<!-- FIGJAM_PALETTE:BEGIN -->
110|| Role | Fill | Stroke | Text on fill | Stroke on canvas |
111||---|---|---|---|---|
112|| Light green | `#CDF4D3` | `#66D575` | 13.87:1 | 1.85:1 |
113|| Light teal | `#C6FAF6` | `#5AD8CC` | 14.61:1 | 1.73:1 |
114|| Light blue | `#C2E5FF` | `#3DADFF` | 12.66:1 | 2.44:1 |
115|| Light violet | `#DCCCFF` | `#874FFF` | 11.21:1 | 4.57:1 |
116|| Light pink | `#FFC2EC` | `#F849C1` | 11.26:1 | 3.13:1 |
117|| Light red | `#FFCDC2` | `#FF7556` | 11.72:1 | 2.65:1 |
118|| Light orange | `#FFE0C2` | `#FF9E42` | 13.25:1 | 2.05:1 |
119|| Light yellow | `#FFECBD` | `#FFC943` | 14.28:1 | 1.53:1 |
120|| Light gray | `#D9D9D9` | `#B3B3B3` | 11.81:1 | 2.1:1 |
121|| Lane | `#F5F5F5` | `#B3B3B3` | 15.29:1 | 2.1:1 |
122|<!-- FIGJAM_PALETTE:END -->
123|
124|### What a `style` line means
125|
126|A user flow or a process may carry one `style` line, or several on nodes that share one pair. The composer reads it as meaning, not as paint:
127|
128|| Where it sits | Pair | What the board shows |
129||---|---|---|
130|| On an end | Light red | An error, in light red, with the pink outline |
131|| On an end | Any other pair | The goal, in light green, with the pink outline, and the spine runs to it |
132|| On a decision | Any pair | The decision keeps its light yellow diamond and takes the pink outline |
133|| On a step | Any pair | That step in focus, in light pink |
134|
135|Pick the node the board exists to explain first, then the line that says what it is. A user flow and a process each need one such line, because the board has no other way to say what the first glance is, and the check refuses a model without one. With no end styled, the end the longest path reaches is still the goal and the others leave the flow, but the goal then carries no outline. A `linkStyle` line passes the check and changes nothing on a composed board, because a connector's colour belongs to its kind, and it never counts as the accent. An architecture, a sequence, a state diagram, an ER diagram and a gantt chart take no `style` line, because their kinds already carry their colour, and the check refuses styling on an architecture.
136|
137|### The accent
138|
139|The first glance is the one node, message or task a reader should see within two seconds, and the accent is how the board says so. Three measures keep it first:
140|
141|- **A hue no kind uses.** The light pink pair belongs to the accent alone and every kind draws another pair. The nearest kind hues, light red at 52 degrees and light violet at 60, sit well clear of the accent's 319
142|- **Weight as well as colour.** A marked node or bar takes an 8 pixel outline against 2 for every other node and 4 for a critical bar, and a marked message takes 4 pixels against 2. On a greyscale copy pink and light blue are both just grey, so the line is what tells them apart. Weight times contrast on white puts 25.0 on the accent against 4.9 on the start pill and 12.6 on the heaviest other mark, the ring of an end state
143|- **The mark gate.** The pink stroke measures 3.13:1 on white, which only violet also clears, so it is the one outline on the board that holds at overview zoom
144|
145|The start pill keeps its light blue, because at those weights it cannot outweigh the accent in colour or in greyscale. What carries the accent depends on the type:
146|
147|| Type | What carries the accent | How the model says so |
148||---|---|---|
149|| User flow, process | A node: a step, a decision, the goal or an error end | A `style` line, which the check requires |
150|| Architecture, state, ER | A node | `%% focus: <id>`, optional |
151|| Sequence | A message | `%% focus: <number>`, the message's place in the order, optional |
152|| Gantt | A task or a milestone | `%% focus: <id or name>`, optional |
153|
154|A `%% focus:` line is a comment, so the Mermaid stays plain. It names one thing, and a second line, a name that matches nothing or a line on a user flow or a process is refused. Where a type carries no focus line the first glance is whatever the layout shows first, and the gate says so. A planned first glance is one thing, never a group such as the end states, and when the layout would show another first, the model names it with a focus line rather than promise a glance the board does not give.
155|
156|### Note palettes
157|
158|The composer and a note extension both set colour through the Plugin API, where FigJam recognises a colour as a palette swatch only when each channel is written as `hex/255`. A rounded decimal makes it a custom colour that the colour picker no longer offers.
159|
160|| Node | Palette |
161||---|---|
162|| Sticky | White `#FFFFFF`, gray `#E6E6E6`, green `#B3EFBD`, teal `#B3F4EF`, blue `#A8DAFF`, violet `#D3BDFF`, pink `#FFA8DB`, red `#FFB8A8`, orange `#FFD3A8`, yellow `#FFE299` |
163|| Section | White `#FFFFFF`, light gray `#F9F9F9`, light green `#EBFFEE`, light teal `#F1FEFD`, light blue `#F5FBFF`, light violet `#F8F5FF`, light pink `#FFF0FA`, light red `#FFF5F5`, light orange `#FFF7F0`, light yellow `#FFFBF0` |
164|| Label | Violet fill `#874FFF`, stroke `#5427B4`, white text, the one preset for numbered pins |
165|
166|Sticky colours keep FigJam's usual meanings: blue for discussion, yellow for a question, green for a positive, pink for a concern, red for a blocker and teal for a decision. One sticky colour per legend is the default, because the numbers already tell the stickies apart.
167|
168|---
169|
170|## 4. GATES
171|
172|| Gate | Threshold | Applies to |
173||---|---|---|
174|| Text on fill | 4.5:1 | Charcoal `#1E1E1E` on every fill the check accepts |
175|| Mark on canvas | 3.0:1 | A stroke that carries meaning, measured on a white canvas |
176|| Text on mark | 4.5:1 | The white digit on a label pin: 4.57:1 on violet `#874FFF` |
177|
178|### Recorded departures
179|
180|| Departure | Measures | Note |
181||---|---|---|
182|| Seven strokes on the canvas | 1.53:1 to 2.65:1 | Every stroke but violet and pink sits under the mark gate. They are FigJam's own pairs, kept so a reader can recolour them from the picker, and the check never lets colour carry meaning alone |
183|| The lane stroke `#B3B3B3` | 2.1:1 | A lane outline is a container edge, not a mark, and its label names it |
184|| Figma's blue label example | Not used | Its white digit on `#3DADFF` measures 2.44:1, under the text gate, so the label pin takes the violet preset |
185|| The saturated fills | Not accepted | FigJam sets white text on a saturated fill, which measures 1.85:1 on `#66D575`. Mermaid cannot set a text colour, and the generator's text colour on a saturated fill was never observed, so the check refuses them |
186|
187|The canvas is measured as white. FigJam's canvas is near white with a dot grid, and its exact value was not measured, so a stroke reads a little weaker on the board than the column says.
188|
189|---
190|
191|## 5. TYPE AND GRID
192|
193|sk-design-diagram's type ramp and grid carry over, because the composer sets the font itself. Every board uses one family at one scale, Inter unless a design names another. A family FigJam cannot load falls back to Inter with a warning:
194|
195|| Text | Size | Weight |
196||---|---|---|
197|| Title | 64 | Bold |
198|| Subtitle | 28 | Regular, wrapped at the diagram's width between 960 and 1440 pixels and then narrowed while it keeps its number of lines, so its lines come out even |
199|| Zone and key names | 24 | Semi Bold |
200|| Node label | 20 | Medium |
201|| Edge label, key entry, source line | 18 | Medium on a connector, Regular elsewhere |
202|| Entity field | 16 | Regular |
203|| Gantt bar length, step pin | 14 | Medium |
204|
205|Every position and size sits on an 8 pixel grid. A shape grows from its kind's base size until its label fits inside it, with a 32 pixel inset in a round shape whose text FigJam clips to the inscribed box, and every shape of one kind on a board takes the size of the largest, so a rank reads as one row.
206|
207|The scale is tuned for a laptop at overview zoom. Reading distance does not change it, as `references/flow-mode.md` Section 4 sets out, and buys fewer nodes and shorter labels instead.
208|
209|A design re-maps meanings onto the pairs in Section 3 and never adds a colour. A board is shared and recoloured in FigJam, so a brand palette would turn every swatch into a custom colour. A brand colour asked for by name is a hand edit after the write, and the reply says it is off-palette.
210|
211|---
212|
213|## 6. WHAT HOLDS THE RECORD
214|
215|- `scripts/figjam_checks/common.py` holds the pairs the check accepts
216|- `assets/figjam-design.md` holds the design a board is drawn in, and `scripts/figjam_checks/design.py` reads it, checks every token against its floor and sends the composer only what differs from the built-in design
217|- `assets/compose-board.js` holds the built-in design, the swatches, the tints and the shapes, and `scripts/compose_board.py --self-test` measures the accent's hue, weight and ink on every board it composes and fails when the design file leaves out a token or breaks a floor
218|- `scripts/compose_board.py --design-check` prints the resolved design with its measured ratios and names every design warning
219|- The self-test fails when the record above names a pair the check does not accept, or the check accepts one the record does not name
220|- The self-test re-measures both ratio columns of every row and fails on any drift
221|
222|---
223|
224|## 7. SPACING
225|
226|Colour tells a reader what belongs together, but space tells them first. A reader groups what sits close before reading a label, so a board that spaces every gap the same reads as one flat field and its own structure disappears.
227|
228|| Band | Gap | What the gap separates |
229||---|---|---|
230|| One thought | 60 to 92 pixels | Two nodes a reader takes as one step or one idea |
231|| Same topic | 200 to 400 pixels | Two groups the board discusses one after the other |
232|| Another part of the board | 1000 pixels or more | Content that answers a different question |
233|
234|Two rules follow from the bands:
235|
236|- Two unrelated groups are never closer than the text blocks inside a card, so the gap between groups always reads wider than the gap within one
237|- A wrapper is larger than the group's own internal gap and smaller than the gap to the next group, so its edge never falls on a neighbour

# use_figma — Figma Plugin API Skill for FigJam

This skill contains FigJam-specific context for the `use_figma` MCP tool. The [figma-use](../figma-use/SKILL.md) skill provides foundational context for plugin API execution via MCP as well as the full Figma plugin API for more advanced use-cases that are not described here.

**Always include `figma-use-figjam` in the comma-separated `skillNames` parameter when calling `use_figma` for FigJam operations. If this skill was loaded via an MCP resource, you MUST prefix the name with `resource:` (e.g. `resource:figma-use-figjam`).** This is a logging parameter used to track skill usage — it does not affect execution.

> **FigJam URL is `figma.com/board/...`.** Do NOT call `figma.createPage()` in FigJam — it throws `TypeError: figma.createPage no such property 'createPage' on the figma global object`. `createPage()` is a Design-file API only (`figma.com/design/...`). FigJam files have a single implicit page; organize content with sections instead (see [create-section](references/create-section.md)).

## Inspecting FigJam Files

**`get_figjam` is the inspection tool for FigJam files.** It returns the full node tree as XML, including IDs of pages, sections, stickies, connectors, and other nodes you need to reference in subsequent `use_figma` calls.

- **Use `get_figjam` upfront** before writing any `use_figma` code that needs to reference existing nodes (page IDs, section IDs, etc.). Don't try to discover IDs by running an inspection script — `console.log` output from `use_figma` is **not returned to the agent** (see [figma-use Critical Rule #4](../figma-use/SKILL.md)). Only the `return` value comes back.
- **`get_metadata` does NOT work on FigJam files** — it is design-mode only and will fail immediately with "unsupported for FigJam files".
- **`get_screenshot` requires a valid `nodeId`** — passing an empty nodeId returns "invalid nodeId" error. Get IDs from `get_figjam` first.
- If you forgot to `return` an ID from a previous `use_figma` call and need it now, call `get_figjam` rather than re-running an inspection script.

## Loading Reference Docs Efficiently

Load only the references your task needs — but when you do need to load multiple, **issue all reads in a single parallel tool-call batch**, not sequentially across turns. For a typical board-creation task, that means a single message containing reads for `plan-board-content` plus the 3-4 specific node-type references you'll use.

## Deferred Tools — Batch-Load Schemas

The Figma MCP tools (`use_figma`, `get_figjam`, `get_screenshot`, `get_metadata`, `create_new_file`, `whoami`) often appear as deferred tools that require `ToolSearch` to load their schemas before they can be called. **Load all schemas in a single `ToolSearch` call** using the `select:` syntax instead of one call per tool:

```
ToolSearch query="select:use_figma,get_figjam,get_screenshot,get_metadata,create_new_file"
```

Six sequential `ToolSearch` calls is six round trips before any work happens. One batched call is one round trip.

## Text Mutations — Canonical Recipe

Every FigJam text mutation (sticky/shape/label/table cell/connector text, standalone text nodes) follows the same recipe as Design files: load font → `await` → mutate → return affected IDs. Skipping the load throws `Cannot write to node with unloaded font "<family> <style>"`. See [figma-use → gotchas.md → Canonical text-edit recipe](../figma-use/references/gotchas.md#canonical-text-edit-recipe-font-load--await--mutate--return-ids). FigJam-specific note: sublayer defaults vary (sticky → `Inter Medium`, shape → `Inter Medium`, connector → invalid until set), so always load from `node.text.fontName` rather than hardcoding `{ family: 'Inter', style: 'Regular' }`.

## Adding Images to a FigJam Board

**`upload_assets` is the ONLY supported way to add images to a FigJam file.** Call `upload_assets` with the FigJam `fileKey`; the tool returns single-use upload URLs that you POST raw image bytes to, and the image is committed and placed automatically. Pass `nodeIds` (with one entry per upload) to attach uploads to existing FigJam nodes as fills; omit `nodeIds` to drop the images onto the board as new layers.

For the full request/response shape, see [figma-use → api-reference.md → Images](../figma-use/references/api-reference.md#images).
